en: *Looking at Fate: A Single Palm’s Gold*.
Master Yi Xing of the Tang dynasty said: "Whenever one seeks a teacher to leave the household life, one must rely on this *Selection Chart for Monks* (*Xuan Seng Tu*) for selection.

Only if one or two who possess discernment are found may one be permitted to leave the household life; if there are none at all who possess discernment, they will instead slander this teaching and [the Buddha]."
The erroneous teachings of the holy ones concern only immediate matters and do not know the final stroke; all ten consciousnesses are the fixed karma of previous lives.

Those who lack even one or two of these consciousnesses have deeply rooted sins and cannot be saved—except for those whose character is extraordinary and far surpasses the common crowd, whom we shall not discuss here. As for the method of observing the ten consciousnesses, it requires years of practice.

The method for taking the *yuezhang tu* (moon-palace chart) from below is as follows: first, calculate the year; from the year, calculate the month; from the month, calculate the day; and from the day, calculate the hour.

Second, calculate the year; from the year, calculate the month; from the month, calculate the day; and from the day, calculate the hour. Third, calculate as before until each calculation reaches the hour.

When the movement (*xingyun*) occurs—whether it be the movement of a single year or the movement of a single hour—the celestial star in the position immediately preceding it is the sequence; follow this pattern for every movement.

For the seven-year *liúnián* (flowing year), calculate the stellar positions starting from the position of the *yùnwèi* (destiny station); for the lunar month, calculate the stellar positions starting from the year of the *liúnián*.
For males, the movement is clockwise; for females, it is counter-clockwise. Thus, good and bad fortune may be verified.

Within the twelve palaces, one goes forth and returns; there is only the repeated wandering across mountains and rivers throughout the world.
All matters of fortune and misfortune are fully discernible within a single palm-stroke of this mountain monk.
*The Golden Palm-Stroke for Examining Fate*, newly carved;
composed by the Śākya monk Yixing of the Tang dynasty.
Ming Dynasty: Hu Family, Wenhui Hall Edition.
The Buddhist and Daoist charts indicate that the Tiangui Star falls upon the Tiangui Palace during this hour; throughout one's life, one will be pure and noble, with harmonious affairs.
One whose ambition and spirit are extraordinary rises above the common crowd; their nature is serene, self-possessed, and luminously penetrating.
The person presided over by this star is pure, noble, virtuous, and upright in conduct; great undertakings succeed, and minor calamities do not invade them.

If further aided by Tianquan (Heavenly Power) and Lùyì (Stationary Star), they will enjoy honor, prosperity, and wealth. Should they encounter a grave transgression, it will primarily result in sorrowful weeping.

If those with the destiny of "Regret," "Middle-Lower," or "Small Person" and "Half-Auspicious" encounter the "Orphaned Calamity" or "Broken Blade" illuminating their destiny, they will certainly be individuals who suffer setbacks at court;
though they may meet with the noble, it will not be entirely auspicious.
When the star of calamity for the celestial realm of hungry ghosts falls upon a person, their nature becomes muddled and chaotic; though they act with alertness, they remain foolish and dull-witted.
Such a person carries an ailment yet manages to prolong their life, provided they must labor diligently to sustain themselves.
If this star is in the house of longevity and the native suffers from illness, and it encounters a "broken blade" (po-ru) star in opposition, the calamity and disease will surely be severe.
If it encounters a powerful or noble star, the native’s illness will be slight; such is a middling-to-superior destiny.

If it encounters a solitary, wayfaring, or treacherous star, the native will be hesitant in all undertakings, will chatter incessantly throughout life, and will certainly suffer setbacks and depart from their ancestral home; such is a middling-to-inferior destiny.
When the Tianquan star and its hour-stem fall upon the Tianquan palace in the human destiny, one’s character is resolute and their willpower is heroic;
they may be somewhat slow in their actions, yet people delight in them, and with a single call there is a hundred responses— truly possessing a majestic air.
If this star is in the house of destiny, the person will be intelligent, brilliant, and refined, possessing influence and power, as well as great wisdom and capability.

If it is assisted by noble, fortunate, or long-lived stars, everyone will listen with respect; however, if it is repeatedly afflicted, one possesses power yet lacks true authority, which is merely a middling destiny.
If it encounters calamity, destruction, isolation, or the "post station" (yi) in the house of destiny, all undertakings will require great effort.
Wealth and riches do not accumulate; one has not yet attained what could have been attained beforehand, nor has one met those with whom one should have met.
One’s life is spent drifting amidst the common masses.
When the star Tianpo (Heaven-Break) falls upon the Tianpo palace during the birth hour, it signifies that the accumulation of gold and jade will ultimately become empty.
Sleeping at night while calculating charts for family wealth—no one knows there are woodworms in the money bag.
This star presides over empty coffers and the dissipation of ancestral estates; yet, if aided by the auspicious stars of those in power, one may still attain a middling lifespan.
Should one encounter the "post-sword" (yìrèn) or "solitary calamity" (gūè) with severe transgressions, undertakings will be arduous and ruin will follow in succession.
Wandering aimlessly from east to west is the destiny of one’s lower lot.
The celestial demons of the asura path are stars whose magnitude is as vast as the great ocean yet as fine as a hair; the Buddha’s mouth is a coiled heart, a double-edged blade on both sides.
Deceitful and crafty, harboring poisonous intent within their schemes; with many shifting thoughts, they are most difficult to harmonize.

When this star illuminates one’s destiny, the individual will experience a lifetime of toil and bustle, rushing about from east to west, speaking one thing while pointing toward another; their guile and transformations are unfathomable.

However, if they receive the assistance of Tian Gui (Heavenly Noble) or Fu Xing (Fortune Star), their wealth and resources will be abundant, constituting a superior destiny. Should they encounter... [text ends]
One born under the star Quanren (權刃) will certainly be a treacherous and cruel petty person;

their words are pure but their conduct is turbid, they are stubbornly malicious and possess a harmful intent toward others, lacking the capacity for tolerance. Their greed and anger are excessive, and they are not a virtuous person.
If they encounter the "Isolated Calamity" (孤厄) or the "Broken Post Station" (破驛), they will surely become a petty person characterized by stinginess, greed, and jealousy; this is a low destiny.
In the Way of the Immortals, celestial phenomena and stellar destiny meet with refined heavenly qi and purity; one is intelligent, wise, and possesses a clear and alert mind.
Men possess talent and women possess elegance, their persons are pure and auspicious, and they fill their bellies with literary works that form a tapestry of brocade.
When this star illuminates one's destiny, the person will be intelligent, clever, and possess learning that surpasses others; their undertakings will be harmonious and auspicious.

If they encounter the assistance of the Tiangui (Heavenly Noble), Tianfu (Heavenly Fortune), or Tianyi (Heavenly Art) stars, they will surely become a leader among the elite, ranking first on the tiger list, and attain the status of one who ascends the golden steps and jade stairs.
If they encounter the Tianquan (Heavenly Power) or Tianren (Heavenly Blade) stars, they will be a man of many talents in both civil and military affairs.
Regarding those with superior destiny, they may encounter the breaking of calamities at solitary stations; as for those who commit grave offenses, they will have studied much but achieved little,

and being not the sort to engage in writing, calculation, or literary pursuits, they will surely become wanderers across lakes and seas— these are the lowest destinies among those skilled in the arts.
The Buddha-way and celestial fortune meet with heavenly blessings at birth; Surely the granaries and treasuries will be overflowing,
With a foundation of vast magnanimity and stability, Wealth and splendor shall flourish, and blessings shall be complete.

If this star sits in the house of the lord of the natal year, the native will receive blessings and enjoy leisure, with a nature that is free and at ease, a broad and magnanimous disposition, and a stable foundation.

Furthermore, being supported by the "Power" (Quan) and "Blade" (Ren) stars, their clothing and silk will be abundant, their storehouses overflowing, and they will possess a destiny of piling up gold and accumulating jade.

However, if it commits a grave offense, their wealth and emoluments will not be great; if it encounters the "Stationary Solitary" (Yi Gu) or "Deceit and Ruin" (Jian Po) stars, it will inevitably presage [misfortune].
A destiny characterized by stinginess, greed, jealousy, and hardship regarding clothing and sustenance.
If a human destiny encounters the Tianyi Star (Heavenly Station Star) in the path of ghosts, one will constantly move and depart from one's ancestral home, never remaining still.
Body and mind find not a moment’s peace; One wanders to the ends of the earth, yet the feet find no rest.
When this star illuminates one's destiny, the master leaves his home and well; The bonds of flesh and blood grow thin, and body and mind are burdened with toil.

For those whose destiny is self-made and independent, if they encounter stars of fortune, power, nobility, wealth, longevity, or learning, it will surely presage the provision of official rank and emoluments.
To have carriages and horses following one is a mandate for honor and distinction;

yet if one encounters the stars of isolation or ruin, it is like leaves blown by the wind or duckweed floating on water—the heart-monkey and will-horse gallop without rest. To wander beyond the secular world, traversing rivers and lakes, is the lot of such a person.
If one further incurs heavy offenses or the calamity of blades that bring mutual injury, they will surely be subject to penal servitude or exile.
If one encounters this "Heavenly Solitude" (*tiān gū*) during the hour of the Human Way (*rén dào*), one will be as if without six types of kin or brothers.
One will certainly become a pure guest at the gate of emptiness; even if one has a wife and children, their emotional ties will be sparse.
When this star illuminates one's destiny, a man will remain solitary throughout his life and lack close relatives;
a woman will suffer the loss of her children and the hindrance of her husband. However, if this "solitary star" (ku-xing) is heavily afflicted, it does not result in solitude;

rather, the person becomes half-monk and half-layman—one whose body remains within the secular world while their heart dwells in the gates of emptiness. If such a person receives the assistance of stars of power, fortune, nobility, or longevity, they will attain the highest status.

Even by fate, one cannot escape the punishments and constraints of youth; if one encounters the stars of broken stations, treacherous calamities, or blades, one's life will surely be adrift on the clouds and waters.
In general, when selecting the destiny of those from ancient houses, one must examine whether the solitary star serves as the primary influence.
The Heavenly Star Tianren (Heavenly Blade) in the Path of Animals: those born under this star are by nature too rigid;
they spend their days debating right and wrong, striving for superiority, wielding knives and axes with severe intent toward their own hearts, much like a general entering the battlefield.
When this star illuminates one’s life, the person will possess a lifelong character that is stubborn and fierce, impetuous and self-opinionated;
they will not tolerate being touched by others and cannot endure idle provocations. Their temperament is like wind and fire, yet they remain upright and free from trouble.

If they encounter the stars of power and fortune, they become extraordinary people whose propriety and righteousness are sufficient to transform the violent; such is a superior destiny. However, if they meet with the stars of isolation and ruin, they will turn treacherous.
Those with great misfortune, coarse minds, and deformed bodies cannot avoid shaving their hair and facing death; this is the destiny of the lower life.
Those with few malefic stars but many auspicious stars also attain the middle life; however, if they commit grave offenses, they will certainly suffer from physical deformity.
The path of the asuras and the heavens, the stars, and the arts;
human nature is most intelligent, yet it can mistake south for north and display many talents.
Its skillful means and clever mechanisms are employed everywhere to harmonize with others and labor diligently in all affairs.
When this star illuminates one's natal lot, the individual will possess great wisdom and many skills, being ingenious and close to the noble.

However, if it is heavily afflicted, the person's natural disposition will be dull, indolent, and stubborn; though they may study much, they will achieve little, becoming a mere laborer in the artisan's trade.

If, however, it receives the favor of celestial power and nobility, blessings, wealth, and longevity will all be complete; with a balance of strength and flexibility, even in the arts, one may achieve success. If...

If one encounters Tiangu (Heavenly Solitude), they may become an extraordinary monk or Daoist; this is a middle destiny. If one encounters Po'e (Broken Calamity), their arts and studies will not succeed, and they will ultimately have a low destiny.
Xian Dao (Immortal Way) is the Tian Shou (Heavenly Longevity) star.
The lifespan of those born under this celestial influence is the longest among men; they are respectful toward superiors and reverent toward inferiors, possessing a nature that is gentle and kind.
Upon hearing something once, they awaken to a thousand points; their hearts are benevolent and compassionate. Between joy and anger, they maintain self-command.

When this star shines upon one’s destiny, the person enjoys longevity and robust health, is wise and intelligent, conducts affairs with gentleness and kindness, and possesses the power to save others.
A person whose heart harbors no intent to harm others will find resentment arising even from acts of kindness;

yet one who conducts affairs with simplicity and sincerity will be revered by all, remaining peaceful throughout their life from beginning to end. Such a person does not manifest joy or anger outwardly.

If they obtain the power of Heaven and the assistance of the stars of fortune and nobility, they will surely possess a broad and magnanimous nature, with blessings and longevity extending far. Those who commit grave offenses may have long lives but lack blessings. Those who commit minor offenses may have neither.
The "Solitary" (*gu*) and "Broken" (*po*) calamity stars correspond to the life-destiny (*ming*).

In the general discussion of the twelve houses, one should know that the method for observing destiny must first take the numerical limits of the life-destiny house as primary; for men, they fear the "solitary" (*gu*) and "stationary" (*yi*) malefic stars.
If one has the Tianfu (Heavenly Fortune) and Tiangui (Heavenly Nobility) stars, there will be no hindrance to their daughter’s fortune;

if one has the Tianquan (Heavenly Authority) star, it assists the husband and brings prosperity to the children; if one has the Tianwen (Heavenly Literature) and Tianyi (Heavenly Artistry) stars, their nature will be clever;

if one has the Tianfu, Tiangui, and Tianshou (Heavenly Longevity) stars, their destiny will be stable and solid; however, if one possesses the Tianjian (Heavenly Deceit) star and commits grave offenses, they will certainly be destined for poverty, lowliness, lewdness, and disgrace.

If the patriarchal destiny encounters a double [configuration], it is a period of great obscurity; if one encounters the calamity stars of *gu* (loneliness) and *po* (ruin) during the month of the life-limit, this month will likewise preside over misfortune.
For a male destiny, a double *Tian-gui* (Celestial Honor) results in being honored yet not truly honored;

a double *Tian-quan* (Celestial Authority) results in possessing authority yet lacking true power; and a double *Tian-wen* (Celestial Culture) leads to excessive indulgence for both men and women. For a female destiny, *Tian-gui* [is similarly interpreted].

If those of heavy [karmic] weight ultimately permit themselves to be esteemed, and if one is seen to esteem the four heavy [sins], then although they may lose their children, their clothing and provisions will be abundant and their heavenly fortune profound.
For those whose heavenly fortune is heavy, clothing and provisions come naturally; yet for those whose heavy [weight] lies in the timing of the days, it conversely does not become a calamity.

One who encounters the three calamities not only lacks calamity, but clothing and provisions will be in surplus. As for those whose life-limit has the Tianquan (Heavenly Power) star, they possess empty nobility and undergo punishment.

Regarding the four calamitous stars that afflict the wife and harm the children: those who possess two "Wealth and Rank" (Yilü) stars will have more than sufficient clothing and provisions for their two sons;
those with two "Power" (Quánxīng) stars will be robust, dignified, and upright; those with three "Power" stars will certainly hold positions of authority and influence.

Those with two "Heavenly Breaker" (Tiānpòxīng) stars will have stable clothing and provisions; those with three "Breaker" (Pòxīng) stars will suffer ruin and decline; those with four "Breaker" stars will lack even basic clothing.

One who has the Star of Fortune (*lù*) but not longevity will have a short life; if the Star of Deceit (*jiān xīng*) appears with double weight, one may instead be upright and honest rather than deceitful.
One with three Stars of Deceit is a crafty and base person; one with four Stars of Deceit likewise presides over exile and penal ruin.

When the Star of Culture (*wén xīng*) is double-weighted, it presides over wealth and nobility; when there are three Stars of Culture, one has little fortune or salary but much learning; with four Stars of Culture, one attains great literary renown.
One who harms his wife and loses his eyesight possesses two fortune stars; one who harms his wife yet attains noble status possesses three fortune stars;

one who has longevity but lacks fortune possesses four fortune stars; one whose clothing and emoluments are abundant possesses two station stars; one who instead lives in peace and leisure possesses three station stars;

one who is subject to lowliness possesses four station stars; and one who gains the labor of servants possesses two orphan stars; one who has sons and grandsons possesses [the corresponding number of] orphan stars.

The three solitary stars mean that a woman will overcome her husband and a man will overcome his son; the four solitary stars mean that the wife will be impoverished; the two-edged stars mean that one is highly charitable;
the three-edged stars mean that one is a noble person with a destiny of power; the four-edged stars mean that one is powerful and noble but short-lived;
and the two-skilled stars mean that one will harm one’s wife and overcome one’s son; the three-skilled stars mean that one is blind or has impaired vision.

1. The "Dull and Ignorant Four Arts" star: one leaps forward in pursuit of learning but achieves nothing. 2. The "Second Longevity" star: one is by nature dull-witted and simple. 3. The "Third Longevity" star: one leaves the household life and attains a long lifespan. 4. The "Fourth Longevity" star:
one departs from their ancestral home and suffers in poverty and misery. The "Noble Station" star: there are two layers of heavy toil and labor. The "Broken" star:

if one encounters a literary talent, they will surely die young; if one encounters power, they will suffer much punishment and conflict. The "Two Orphans" star: it brings about mutual punishment and strife.

Though the person’s years may be advanced, they will suffer ruin and incur blame; those with a heavy burden of "double-edged blades" (rengan) are stingy and greedy, and their blessings shall not endure long.

If one encounters a "double-edged blade," there will be injury, ruin, and decay; if one encounters a "blade" (rengan), there will be calamity, illness, and poverty. If one encounters both calamities at birth, death will occur in early life;
if three "solitary pillars" (sagi) appear in the four pillars, there will be ruin in middle age. When the "blade" and "calamity" occupy the same house, the same misfortunes follow.

If one harms oneself, it will injure one's hands and feet; if the noble longevity and the power of the year-month are abundant, one’s ancestral estate will surely flourish and the family lineage will be distinguished.
When the calamity of broken blades and solitary misfortune converge at once, it is difficult to maintain a harmonious marriage or have offspring.

The principles of the twelve lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are fully contained herein; when discussing the destiny of a lifetime, who could have any doubt? Let the wise examine this carefully and deduce its implications in detail.
By this, one may investigate fortune and misfortune through foreknowledge.

According to the discourse on birth in the twelve months, those born in the first month have a destiny favorable to officialdom and proximity to the noble; they accomplish great matters through small means, and their nature is characterized by meticulousness and caution, which can attract [favor].
Wealth from all four directions, harmony between wife and children, and no mutual conflict or destruction.
For those born in the first month, their dignified appearance is the result of past affinities; throughout life they shall enjoy happiness and their blessings shall be continuous.
Noble people will welcome and guide you, increasing auspiciousness; may you live in harmony and reunion for a hundred years.
Born in the second lunar month, your nature is gentle and your heart free from malice; you are intelligent and possess great wisdom.
You have little affinity with your six relations, yet in the middle period of your life you will attain wealth and great prosperity. This is a destiny that is half-true and half-false.
Those born in the second month of the lunar calendar are by nature good throughout their lives, as they know this within themselves. Their clothing and provisions are naturally abundant;
with wealth in money and grain and many family treasures, they shall be noble and honored, yet may be slighted by the lowly.

Those born in the third month possess a nature that is broad and magnanimous, enduring all matters with patience. Their destiny is one of moderate fortune in the first period, the development of blessings in the middle period, and glory, wealth, and nobility in the final period.
A verse on those born in the third month:
A person whose mind is straightforward naturally possesses a broad heart; throughout their life they attract wealth from all quarters.
In the middle years, when prosperity flourishes, blessings manifest like withered trees meeting the spring.

In the fourth month, the human nature becomes unsettled, causing one's reputation to move through the four directions; they form friendships with ease but do not remain settled in their ancestral estate.
Regarding the family tradition of self-reliance: the first limit is middling, the middle limit is ordinary, and the final limit brings great prosperity and noble status.
For those born in the fourth month, the destiny for the first year of life is superior to that of subsequent years; there is no need for resentment, bitter grief, or anxious torment.
Furthermore, one shall obtain the merit of the expedient means of observing the fast; husband and wife shall live in harmony and remain forever united.
Those born in the fifth month are gentle and kind by nature, possessing a sharp and clever mind; they have power and prestige, their conduct is upright, and they are guided by noble persons.
However, such individuals are fated to experience a separation from their spouse midway through their lives.
For those born in the fifth month, their travels and comings-and-goings often encounter unexpected windfalls; noble persons welcome them with smiling faces.
Their agricultural and business enterprises flourish greatly, and wealth, honor, and splendor arrive in succession.
Those born in the sixth month are naturally skillful and clever, possessing far-reaching insight and personal arts; they do not adhere to their ancestral occupations.
They have wealth at the beginning, prosperity during the middle period, and nobility in the final period. Because their strategic ingenuity is profound, this is indeed a fortunate destiny.
For those born in the sixth month,
their life’s clothing and provisions will naturally flourish; they will achieve prominence and excel in literary arts,
living in leisurely happiness with a wealthy and noble family, and enjoying a harmonious old age with their spouse for a full hundred years.

Those born in the seventh month are naturally charitable and kind; they are meticulous in their affairs and fond of beauty. Their first period of life is mediocre, while their middle period is somewhat favorable;
their destiny is one of wealth, nobility, and glory in the final period.
For those born in the seventh month, their life’s work as human beings need not cause anxiety; remain at ease with nothing to trouble the mind.
One should establish one's own household, estate, and fields; only then will one know that fortune and prosperity are sought within one's own destiny.
Those born in the eighth month have eyes with a radiant luster; they are intelligent and comprehend the principles of truth and correctness, being without private bias.
Possessing both arts and wealth, their destiny is to draw near to the nobility. If they are born away from their ancestral home, they will attain great honor.
Those born in the eighth month have poetry as their lot;
they are upright in person with a majestic countenance. Their minds are clever and their natures are kind and good;
they are capable in many undertakings and their hearts comprehend principle. When their fortune arrives in later years, their blessings will be enduring and long-lasting.
Those born in the ninth month are by nature stern and prone to inviting trouble from others; they possess a destiny of authority and proximity to the noble.
Their marital relations will be characterized by mutual incompatibility, resulting in a late marriage and belated offspring.
A verse on those born in the ninth month:
In all matters of buying and selling, one will be strong; in planning and action, one’s ambition will be lofty.
If one can cultivate goodness and perform many meritorious deeds, one will surely find that clothing and provisions fill the chests.

Those born in the tenth month possess a heart like the great ocean—unwavering and untiring; what was difficult at first becomes easy later, and their clothing and emoluments shall suffice for their person.

This is their destiny: the female precedes the male in death; it is difficult for them to serve as teachers and disciples when they leave the household life, and likewise difficult for them to be children or spouses in the household life;
in their fate, they frequently encounter the afflictions of mutual conflict and destruction.
Poem for those born in the tenth month:
Those born in the tenth month celebrate the auspicious star; Calamities shall forever recede and never again invade.
Observing the fasts, practicing wholesome thoughts, and performing acts of kindness, Their clothing and provisions will abound, bringing them natural contentment.
Those born in the eleventh month possess a nature of authority, are quick-witted and clever, have a disposition inclined toward serving the noble, and are full of stratagems.
They may suffer from chronic illness in their person. Their first period of life is mediocre; their middle period brings forth fortune; and their final period is a destiny of wealth and nobility.
The Verse for those born in the eleventh month:
In early years you stand alone, having established your own household; Your clothing and provisions follow your heart’s desire—this is truly praiseworthy.
Flesh and blood brothers and sisters offer no reliance; Friends with whom you associate are like flowers upon the water.
Those born in the twelfth month labor with their hearts for a hundred years; they are straightforward of heart but quick of speech, yet are also prone to chronic illnesses.
It is difficult to rely upon parents and siblings, yet one can obtain clothing, provisions, and wealth from all quarters of one’s own accord. This is a destiny of mixed fortune.
For those born in the twelfth month, the first period of their life is one of diligent toil and bitter suffering; they achieve self-reliance and do not seek the favor of others.
Though kind-hearted, they are quick-tongued and find it difficult to conceal their malice; may they pass several springs in harmony with both elders and juniors.
Discourse on the rotation of auspicious and inauspicious stars within the thirty days of each month relative to the birth date:

For those born on the first, seventh, thirteenth, nineteenth, or twenty-fifth day of the month, the Sun Star (Taiyang Xing) falls upon their day of birth. Such individuals will have an abundance of clothing and emoluments; their initial period of life will be ordinary, while the final period will be... [prosperous].
A man born on the 19th or 25th day of the month, aged between eighteen and twenty-five, is destined for honor and prosperity.
Having both parents and being supported by a capable wife, he possesses a destiny that brings fortune to his husband and bestows blessings. [Favorable days: the 2nd, 8th, 14th, 20th, and 26th.

Those born on this day have the Moon Star (Taiyin) coinciding with the day; such individuals possess refined and elegant character. They may experience the loss of one or both parents and lack support from their six close relatives.
It is difficult to rely upon siblings, yet the male head of the family will be exceptionally distinguished and the female head will be intelligent—a destiny destined for success and establishment.
The third day of the first month, the ninth day of the first month, the fifteenth, the twenty-first, and the twenty-seventh:
those born on these days have the Tianwu Star (Heavenly Warrior Star) presiding over their day. This indicates harmony between husband and wife, yet they will be unable to live together in old age;

there will be no injuries or calamities. In the final stage of life, they will enjoy prosperity, honor, and wealth. However, they will incur offenses, leave their ancestral home, and establish a new household, thereby severing their ancestral legacy.
Fields and gardens will waste away; women will bring harm to their husbands; it will be difficult to obtain offspring, and even if they are obtained, they will suffer separation.
It is not harmful for those who have moved into a new residence. [Auspicious days: The 4th, 10th, 16th, 22nd, and 28th.

For those born on this day, the star of the Mother of Heaven (Tianmu) coincides with the day; such individuals will be highly learned yet achieve little, experience financial hardship in their middle years, and encounter trouble and litigation.
However, their marital relations will be harmonious, and they will enjoy wealth and nobility in their final years—a destiny of great auspiciousness.

Those born on the first, fifth, eleventh, seventeenth, twenty-third, or twenty-ninth days have the Heavenly Emperor Star (Tianhuangxing) coinciding with their birth day; such individuals are clever and intelligent, possessing more than sufficient clothing and sustenance.
They lack close kinship and find it difficult to rely upon brothers, yet their wealth and profit remain undiminished—a destiny of middling fortune.
Those born on the first, twelfth, eighteenth, twenty-fourth, or thirtieth day of the lunar month have the Taiyi Star (Taithi) presiding over their birth day.
Such individuals are generally highly learned and versatile, possessing a destiny of refined leisure, nobility, and literary pursuits.

Their first life-stage (*prathama-avasthā*) is one of great honor; the middle stage is stable and even; and the final stage is one of great prosperity and abundant wealth and emolument. Regarding siblings... [text truncated]

The younger brother said, "It will be fine as long as there is no reliance [on external factors]. Regarding the auspiciousness and misfortune for those born during the twelve periods (*dvādaśa-lagna*), the hour of the Rat (*mūhūrta*) is as follows:
This person is by nature impetuous and their destiny is marked by rigidity; their undertakings are fickle and unstable, inviting trouble from others.
They will experience separation from parents and spouse, yet possess a destiny to build a household with their own hands.
Their lifespan is eleven, eighteen, thirty-six, forty-six, fifty-eight, eighty-nine, or ninety years.
For those born in the Chou hour, their parents will face conflict and suppression; throughout life, they will revere the noble and those with power and influence.
In the final years of their life, their fortune and blessings will be abundant. They will encounter calamities in the years eighteen, twenty-six, thirty-one, and forty-six.
One may observe the fasts and cultivate merit to attain a lifespan of seventy-three years.

Those born in the hour of the Tiger (寅) will likely experience the loss or separation of parents, siblings, wife, or children; it is best to leave one's ancestral home. The first period of life will be mediocre, while the final period will be [prosperous].
At the ages of twenty-six, twenty-nine, thirty-three, thirty-nine, forty-nine, and sixty-six, one will be subject to ailments of the qi and blood;
beyond these, one will reach the lifespan of ninety-six years.

For those born in the hour of the Rabbit (Mao), their parents, siblings, wives, and children will lack strength. During the first and middle periods of life, undertakings will not succeed; only in the final period will there be stability.

Throughout one's life, it is difficult to maintain ancestral property. Those who leave home to become monks or enter a wife’s family as a son-in-law will experience misfortune at first but good fortune later, particularly at ages eighteen or twenty.
There will be calamities during the sixth year, after which one’s lifespan may be extended to ninety years.

Those born in the hour of the Dragon (Chen) will find it difficult for their parents, siblings, wife, and children to remain together; they are naturally intelligent and quick-witted, and will possess wealth in the first period of their life.
The middle period involves loss of wealth; the final period remains as radiant as before. Minor calamities occur at ages nineteen, twenty-seven, thirty-six, and thirty-nine.
Beyond these, one reaches the full lifespan of seventy-five years.
Those born during the Si hour (9–11 am) are intelligent and handsome; their first period is one of glory and prosperity, with abundant clothing and provisions.

They will establish their own industries and estates, though they possess a destiny marked by strife and conflict among kinsmen. There will be calamities at ages thirty-one, thirty-six, and forty-nine; beyond these, they will live for seven [years].
A lifespan of fourteen years.

For those born at noon, their human nature will possess the harmonious energy of a spring breeze, transforming their ancestral legacy; they will experience good fortune during both the initial and middle periods, and it is auspicious for them to maintain [their practice].

If one observes the fast to cultivate merit on the thirteenth, twenty-third, twenty-seventh, thirty-sixth, or forty-ninth day, and falls ill, one will pass away at the hour of Wei (15:00–17:00) at a lifespan of seventy-eight years.
If it exceeds this, one will reach the age of eighty. At the hour of Wei.

A person born with this destiny will have incomplete parents, a marriage subject to mutual conflict and strife, and will achieve success through hard labor. In the first period of life there is wealth;
in the middle period there is alarm and fear; in the final period, wealth and emolument will be abundant. There will be misfortune at ages nineteen, twenty-nine, and fifty-six;
beyond these, the lifespan reaches seventy-three years.

For those born during the Shen hour, departure from one's ancestral home brings good fortune; however, parents and siblings will not all survive, and while the couple will live out their lives together in goodness, the destiny involves proximity to the noble.
The initial period is full of reversals, but the final period is most auspicious—at ages nineteen, twenty-two, twenty-six, and thirty.
At eighty-four, there will be calamities; beyond this, one reaches a lifespan of seventy-seven years.

Those born in the hour of You (酉) are pure and sincere by nature, making it difficult for them to serve as parents or brothers; their first period of life is unstable, while their final period is very auspicious.
The minor calamities occur at twenty-two, twenty-eight, thirty-nine, forty-six, seventy-seven, and seventy-seven years;
this is the period of the hour of the Dog (戌).
This is a destiny for one born with a refined, elegant, and handsome appearance who will experience happiness throughout their life; however, fortune and rank are subject to fluctuations.
The first, second, and third periods (liàn) are peaceful and auspicious, while the final period brings conflict between parents and loss to the spouse.
There will be calamities at ages fourteen, twenty-six, twenty-nine, and thirty-six; beyond these, the lifespan reaches seventy-five years.
Those born at the hour of Hai (9–11 PM) are straightforward in mind and quick of speech; naturally, their fortune and rank will increase.

Although they will experience a lifetime of diligent toil and labor, it is a destiny that is highly auspicious in its final stage, though the ancestral estate will be difficult to maintain during the initial period. [The years of great fortune are] twenty-six, thirty-six, and forty-nine.

Fifty-six minor calamities pass; beyond this, regarding the auspiciousness and misfortune of those born at the beginning, middle, or end of the twelve periods within an eighty-eight-year lifespan, [it is discussed as follows]: Sub-periods (zǐ): 1. The first ten years are the period of the child (*bāla*). 2. From the eleventh year to the twentieth is the period of the youth (*yauvana*). 3. From the twenty-first year to the thirtieth is the period of the adult (*prauḍha*). 4. From the thirty-first year to the fortieth is the period of the elder (*vṛddha*). 5. From the forty-first year to the fiftieth is the period of the declining age (*pariṇata*). 6. From the fifty-first year to the sixtieth is the period of the decrepit (*jīrṇa*). 7. From the sixty-first year to the seventieth is the period of the aged (*vṛddhatara*). 8. From the seventy-first year to the eightieth is the period of the very old (*atīvavṛddha*). 9. From the eighty-first year to the ninetieth is the period of the senescent (*jarātura*). 10. From the ninety-first year to the hundredth is the period of the dying (*mumūrṣu*). 11. From the one-hundred-and-first year to the one-hundred-and-tenth is the period of the deceased (*mṛta*). 12. From the one-hundred-and-eleventh year onwards is the period of the departed (*preta*). In these twelve stages, one should examine the specific characteristics of the birth time to determine whether it is auspicious or inauspicious. If one is born during the initial stage of a period, it is generally favorable; if born during the middle or final stage, there may be obstacles or decline. One must further correlate this with the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the day of the week (*vāra*), and the planetary positions to discern the full extent of fortune and misfortune.
At birth, this person first brings misfortune to their mother; they establish their own household and manage affairs with seven advances and eight retreats, ten successes and nine failures.

Their six kin become distant and indifferent, and their clothing and provisions fluctuate between abundance and scarcity. In the final stage of life, they enjoy blessings, destined for a favorable harvest and a successful conclusion.

Regarding the initial fruits of the Pozi [Poison] school: In undertaking affairs, there is much advancement and retreat; The methods of the masters and the paths of the monks bring good fortune, Yet for a lifetime one endures constant toil and wandering.

Furthermore, he will have a son born before his first child; his offspring shall not exceed two. He will marry a wife who replaces his former one, and in the end, he will distribute his fields and manors.
If a person is born under this [asterism], there will be no mutual overcoming or destruction throughout their life; whatever they undertake will involve both rise and fall, success and failure.
Although they may achieve great prosperity in the end, it is auspicious for them to leave their ancestral home and enter as a son-in-law.
In this verse: Although the Heavenly Steward (Tianlu) is flourishing, it currently occupies the Palace of Vitality (Huoli). Guard against minor losses in your future endeavors;
cultivate merit to ensure prosperity and success.
If the child is born at the end of the month, the person will first overcome their father; the six close relatives will not provide support, and the offspring will be unfilial.

Throughout one's life, there will be diligent toil and labor, with tasks that have a beginning but no end, and wealth and resources will not accumulate. This is a destiny subject to change; the latter years of life will be favorable.
The character for "Poet" (詩) ends with the stroke for "Past" (末), followed by "Ox" (丑). Three descendants shall possess it; A fine son must be one, like the willow in the springtime of old age.

For those born in the first period of the Ox year, there is no mutual overcoming or destruction; they will advance in fields and manors, with clothing and provisions fully provided, enjoying wealth, honor, and peace.
Their descendants will flourish and attain high distinction; this is a destiny that is excellent in its final stage.
The poem says: The late harvest is bountiful; the two sons exchange wives; brothers support one another, and their glory and fortune are equal.
Those born in the Year of the Ox are honest and diligent; they will acquire fields and manors, and their spouses will be supportive from a young age.
Their parents and six relations will live in harmony, and in the final stage of their lives, they possess a destiny for great success and noble wealth.
The second daughter in the year of the Ox must first guard against her father; the eldest son must guard against the injuries of old age.
One must also guard against the wife’s harm, for she may likewise injure one's parents. If one possesses intelligence and wit, fortune, rank, clothing, and grain will increase.
Wealth, silks, and fields shall be vast; glory and splendor flourish in the final years of life.

Those born in the final period of the Ox year have kind and virtuous hearts; though beginning with misfortune, they end in good fortune. Initially, they are destined to lose their mother and live in solitude, yet they achieve success through their own efforts. If male, they will attain self-reliance.
Women all depart from the mandate of their ancestors.
In the *Shijing*, the last line of the "Chou" section states that the mother was killed first; the woman’s fate brings three obstacles to her father—first the man, followed by women.
Those born under the late hours of the evening will have assistance from nobles;

those born at the beginning of the Tiger hour (Yin) will see their fathers pass away early, yet possess abundant fortune and livelihood. Such individuals are intelligent and successful, achieving success through their own efforts.
Established with both abundance and deficiency, the nature of mind is unsettled; one is fond of victory and fond of interruption, yet possesses a destiny of fortune in the final years.
In the first year of the Tiger, fields and manors advance; sons and daughters are joyfully formed as pairs; wealth and rank flourish in middle age.
Those born in the Yin hour during the evening hours of the Kang year will,
if there are no conflicting or destructive influences, have both parents living, enjoy abundant wealth and status, and possess both fortune and longevity.
In establishing a family, there will first be prosperity; in later years, one’s life will be peaceful and stable.
The verse says: "The destiny of the Tiger hour is auspicious and flourishing; one is intelligent with a firm temperament; throughout one's life, it is best to leave the ancestral home."
One's name and lineage will spread in all four directions; one will have younger brothers born in the Year of the Tiger. Three grandchildren will carry on the lineage for generations.
One must be cautious regarding marriage, as it may bring misfortune to the wife; however, wealth will flourish and fields and manors will increase. The year of the Tiger brings prosperity.

Those born in this year will first lose their mother; they must establish themselves independently as their own family, for they lack support from their six relations. Their destiny is to leave their ancestral home and renounce the world.

Throughout their life, they will endure hardship and mental toil. They will suffer the loss of a spouse, but by maintaining a disciplined lifestyle and observing their illnesses, they may extend their lifespan.

The end of the year of the Tiger brings a message of peace; Regarding the ancestral estate, one will not be able to look after it. Throughout one's life there will be many perils and hardships, like a boat breaking upon a high sandbar.
It is better to wait until late to take a son or daughter-in-law; There is no karmic affinity for a first wife at this time.
Brothers have no reliance; the false son is sent back to heaven.

Those born in the first watch of the morning will first overcome their mother. Though clothing and fortune from the four quarters provide assistance, ancestral property once established will again fall into ruin. The work will be done, yet it shall fail.
One whose affairs begin but lack an end has a destiny for which the household budget will naturally sustain itself.
Po Shi was born at the initial hour of the Rabbit (Mao). As a person, he is most solitary and distressed; his clothing and provisions are provided according to the times.
Seeing joy gives rise to sorrow; the twenty lands are established by themselves. Pitiable is the one who overcomes his lawful wife;
brothers shall find no strength. Offspring will certainly be delayed until the year of the Hare.

The destiny of one born in the middle life-span: their life will not suffer ruin or destruction; as the lord of a single lifetime, they shall obtain unexpected wealth that arrives of its own accord without being sought; and their life is one for establishing oneself through martial arts.
Poem:
The wealthy and noble raise high beams; clothing and sustenance are most magnificent. Throughout one’s life, the family estate thrives, and martial arts bring one near to the sovereign.
Offspring form orderly ranks, and the wife is surely wealthy—two such signs appear.
When the stars of the two palaces govern the body and the life-span, brothers stand in distinguished rows.

Those born in the latter part of the Rabbit year will first lose their father; at nineteen, they will achieve success in their undertakings, yet their fortune and status will fluctuate between advancement and decline. Their final life stage will be mediocre.

It is difficult for them to have children, and though their ancestral estate may be extensive, they will not be able to inherit it. They must establish themselves through independent authority and build their own family abroad.
This is the mandate of Heaven.
At the beginning of the poem, there was great toil and hardship; through diligent care, he established his own household. Now that the time has come, one who understands him meets with good fortune.
Withered trees bloom once more; within one's destiny, many brothers abound. The fields and manors belong to others' offspring;
though difficult to rely upon, a virtuous wife is truly praiseworthy.
One born at this time will first bring misfortune to their father; if they are the eldest son, it will certainly be difficult for them to get along with their brothers.

They are intelligent and understand affairs, possessing a compassionate heart and love for others. Great matters will be reduced to small ones, and their clothing and provisions will be ordinary. This is a destiny of self-reliance;
children will be welcomed late in life, and one must leave the ancestral home to live as a son-in-law elsewhere.
Poetry brings clothing and emoluments from all quarters, yet brothers and the six types of kin fall into discord.
Thorns sprout upon level ground, vexing and distressing the heart within; parents lose their long lives early, and wives and children have tears filling their cheeks.
Throughout one's life there will be many reversals; it seems this is destined by fate.

Those born in the Earthly Branch of the Dragon (Chen) will have their primary lord suppress their mother; their clothing and fortune will be mediocre, yet they will establish a mind of public fairness and upright integrity, becoming wealthy in the middle years.
Your noble nature is as impetuous as wind fanning a fire; quick to flare up and quick to subside, you have established your own household. Your wife comes from a high-ranking family;
this is the fate of one who has taken up residence with a beautiful woman as a son-in-law.
A poem.
Day after day one runs in toil and bustle; The source of wealth may come or go.
One's six kin offer no help, and affairs of slander and dispute are ever many. In the Dragon year, there is misfortune regarding wife and official standing.
Grandchildren remain unseen, yet an outsider son inherits the maternal kin. In the final years of life, the status will be most exalted.

Those born in the latter part of the Dragon Hour (Chen) have lives free from fatal conflicts; their character is impartial and fair, their wealth and rank are stable and sufficient, and they enjoy much happiness.
Such is the destiny of one who, like a fish transforming into a dragon, soars through the gates of heaven, manifesting great success and bringing glory to their family.
In the verse: Fish and dragons transform their bodies; clothing and sustenance naturally abound. One day, as thunder and rain arise, one’s fame shakes the four seas.
At the end of the hour-branch, the wife will be harmed; in the Tian-fang mansion, relatives harm each other.
Though one gains strength from one's own children, one is more closely related to an external son;

those born at the beginning of the month first overcome their mother, attaining wealth and nobility in the early years, with land and houses, and possessing the authority to advance or retreat and establish themselves independently.
Fate: This fate transcends the ordinary; In the course of cultivation, one burns fine incense, Yet mother and child are often parted.
The family business begins to flourish; in the first month of the year, descendants appear early. Wild geese do not form their rows;
the fields and gardens advance only to retreat; wealth and silks are like frost at midday.

Born in the middle period of life, one first brings misfortune upon one’s father; throughout one's life, one speaks only of heaven and earth with straightforwardness, yet meddles excessively in others' affairs, leading to many successes and many failures.
One lacks the support of close relatives, yet possesses a spirit that transcends the common crowd—a destiny of such character.

When poetry establishes the person, the self becomes secure; when intention is raised, the mind soars toward the heavens. With courage as vast as the sky, one’s blessings will extend far into the future.
Among the Earthly Branches, this is the Zi (rat) year; it brings hope for one's descendants and presides over the advancement of fields and gardens.
He will overcome his wife and two children, yet his descendants will be virtuous.
Those born later in life will suffer no such losses; clothing and provisions will be abundant, and all brothers will remain together. He is clever by nature and associates with the noble.
If one’s destiny is for the happiness of establishing a family, it will be most auspicious if one leaves the household life.
As the poem concludes: "Joyful with literary arts, establishing a family brings great prosperity; the Moon Palace is but a few inches away."
Established in the station of the noble, at the end of the *si* hour there is immeasurable merit; though the house of the wife may fear injury,
one’s life will be full of joy, and in old age one shall enjoy peace and security during the *wu* hour.

A person born under this sign will not suffer from the afflictions of a lifetime; they will enjoy wealth and honor, being proficient in both civil and military arts. They will be generous and magnanimous by nature, excelling beyond their peers and rising above the crowd.
However, their own six kin will lack the means to support them, and they will have the destiny to establish a household outside their native home.
The poet was born at the very beginning of noon; At his first movement, a hundred people supported him. In a peaceful carriage he sat with horses, manifesting the ways of the noble;
His six kin could not exert their strength, And even his brothers were mostly estranged.
The wife will have many concubines and great wealth; the wealthy household shall possess a thousand servants.

Those born in the hour of Wu (noon) first overcome their father; clothing and fortune are achieved through hardship, with reversals between success and failure. There is difficulty at first, followed by good fortune in the final period of life.
The Destiny of Prosperity:
Poetry says that from birth one lacks freedom; Whether food and clothing are sufficient or not, One passes the days in a state of frantic, petty clamor.
Wherever one displays elegance,

those born in the latter part of the *wu* hour will first lose their mother; lacking support from six types of kin, they will find it difficult to maintain their ancestral estate, and though they toil for clothing and sustenance, they must rely on diligence and frugality.
The destiny for establishing a household lies at the end of one's life.
In the fifth and sixth periods of the poem, the destiny is ordinary; wealth and children pass by according to one's lot. If one seeks further advancement or profit, [it will not be attained].
Throughout one's life, there will be constant奔波 (restlessness/striving);

there is no early death for those just born, and siblings will remain complete. One will be elegant and refined everywhere; beginning with diligence, one later becomes indolent regarding food and clothing.
Sufficient for one’s needs; without seeking, wealth arrives of its own accord. Though there may be hardship at the beginning, fortune increases in later years.
There is no ruin at the start of the verse. Two sons will be brought into the family, and brothers will be united in harmony.
Fields and houses will flourish in later years;

before one reaches middle age, one will first overcome paternal obstacles. Clothing and provisions will come naturally; the mind will be impartial, affairs will be fully managed, and success and fame will follow.
In this destiny of wealth and honor where it is difficult for one's six kin to precede, there is misfortune at first followed by good fortune later.
The poem states that before reaching middle age, one will first lose one’s father; furthermore, it presages injury to the head and loss of a wife; brothers must exercise mutual forbearance.
The son will depend on his mother later in life;
he will die before his mother and attract wealth from the four quarters, yet he shall not obtain the assistance of others. His moods of joy and anger are inconsistent.
One will constantly face the fate of entering a marriage by becoming a son-in-law or leaving home to become a monk.
Poems and clothing, as well as one's livelihood, arrive only occasionally; human affections come and go, and ancestral estates are mostly ruined.
Defeated, he rejoices; in adversity, he turns to sorrow.

Those born in the first period of the Monkey year lack the nature of being overcome or destroyed; they are skillful and intelligent, finding rescue even in calamity, turning great matters into small ones throughout their lives.
A stable and substantial destiny that may cause loss to one's wife and children, yet establishes one’s own family enterprise.
The verse states: "The foundation of one's destiny is flourishing; domestic fortune is abundant; one will early enter the registers of civil and military officials."
Exchanging brocade and embroidery for coarse hempen garments;

those born in the Year of the Monkey will first bring misfortune upon their father. Their six close relatives will lack the power to protect them, leading them to invite trouble and provoke strife. They will be surrounded by petty people, and their clothing and provisions will be insufficient.
There is still life remaining.
Let the poet’s fondness rest here. Do not trust the conduct of petty people; settle your mind and maintain your proper station.
Charitable and benevolent through spring and autumn;

born in the latter part of the month of Shen, one first loses one's mother. One’s six close relatives will not provide support. Marriage should be delayed; one should take a wife from a different surname.
Many people doubt the destiny of one who transforms misfortune into good fortune.
The poem says: Chasing flowers, he abandoned his ancestral estate; Standing alone, he maintained himself in solitude; Born outside the family, he grew old following his mother.

For those born in the first ten days of the month of You (酉) with the final limit of surplus [days]: there will be no destruction or loss; clothing and provisions will be sufficient; they will largely inherit ancestral property; their nature will be skillful and intelligent; as for men—such is the case.
Mastery of both dragon and tiger, both civil and martial; skillful and refined in the feminine arts, one’s later years shall be as one desires.
Poetry:
The Metal destiny shines forth of its own accord; one’s achievements lead to a return in brocade robes, for in strategic planning there is great wisdom.
How could wealth and fortune ever suffer deficiency?

Those born in the Year of the Rooster will first lose their father; their six kin will be discordant, and they should live with those of a different surname, keeping their bodies apart so that their minds may be at peace.
One’s innate character sustains the destiny that brings forth fortune.
One’s poetry, clothing, and emoluments vary somewhat with the times, just like the cock that heralds the dawn, able to crow to urge others to rise early.
One born in the final hour of You (酉) will first lose their mother;

the six close relatives will provide no support. One's temperament is impetuous and remorseless, yet clothing and sustenance will not fail, and there will be no misfortune regarding the metal element (辛).
Regarding the *Rong* (Glory) trigram: one's descendants will find it difficult to flourish, and one’s life will be solitary for many years.

In the *Shiyou* (Wine and Meat) trigram, the son arrives late; one possesses the talent for a pure and lofty renunciation of the household. In the *Qi* (Wife) palace, there is a danger of separation or loss.
It is appropriate to plant fields of merit;

those born at the beginning of the Earth-Branch (Wu) period first overcome their father, and their brothers do not provide support. This is a destiny for associating with the noble, which flourishes in late life.
Blessings come from filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
When one’s conduct is good and upright and one acts according to the Way, Heaven sends down wealth and property; One thus achieves self-reliance through the mandate of fate.
One will always stay close to noble persons;

those born under the Tai and Shu palaces first lose their mother and have no reliance among their six kin. Food and clothing depend upon official circles, and one transforms misfortune into good fortune.
The heart craves pleasure while the mind and gallbladder toil like hemp seeds; the mouth is like one driven mad by the wind—a destiny whose blessings will only manifest at the very end.
A poem:

Amidst the multitude, one attains humility and harmony; receiving imperial grace, one’s emoluments are abundant. With majesty and virtue that others revere, who would dare to transgress when you preside?
(Hài)
One born at this time first brings misfortune to their father, but thereafter accomplishes all endeavors as they wish. Throughout their life, they draw near to the noble;
they possess a destiny endowed with both fortune and longevity.
Poem:
In all matters of elegance and refinement, success in fame and office shall naturally be achieved;
every wish fulfilled, may blessings and longevity fill the green mountains. (Hài)

Those born during this period will not suffer the loss or ruin of their parents; their initial voice will resonate with subsequent sounds in a state of equilibrium and flexibility, allowing them to avoid calamities;
they will draw near to noble persons and possess a destiny for flourishing in their later years.

In the middle of the *shīhài* (癸亥) year, there is no mutual overcoming or destruction; clothing and provisions will be abundant and beneficial; one possesses both authority and power, yet one's temperament and character cannot be fathomed.

Those born at the end of the Hai hour first lose their mother; clothing and fortune follow the seasons, and the six kin are effective. Supported by noble patrons, one should perform meritorious deeds and cultivate the fasts.
In the end, one will obtain noble offspring and possess a destiny of distinguished achievement.
In the twelve hours of the day, at the end of Hai (11–1 p.m.), though clothing and provisions may be meager,
if one is willing to follow the times and cultivate a virtuous heart through the practice of fasting and precepts, one will surely give birth to a noble child who shall come to support them.

If the [lunar] half-month is performed before midnight during the first half of the year, it is the "prior half-month"; if performed after midnight during the second half of the year, it is the "subsequent half-month.

Regardless of whether the person is male or female, among the four characters of the Earthly Branches—zi (rat), yin (tiger), wu (horse), shen (monkey), and xu (dog)—these are Yang; while chou (ox), hai (pig), you (rooster), wei (sheep), si (snake), and mao (rabbit) are Yin.
If the Yang characters predominate and the Yin are few, the child will overcome the father; if the Yin characters predominate and the Yang are few, the child will overcome the mother.
Having grasped this in the mind, one responds with the hand: from the year one ascends to the month, from the month to the day, from the day to the hour, and from the hour to the *ke*.
For men it proceeds in direct order, for women in reverse; encountering the ominous brings misfortune, encountering the noble brings honor.
Within the span of a single movement of fortune, all is illuminated such that nothing can escape it.

In calculating the five life-spans of a person, one must avoid days that correspond to the day of illness or the day of the grave (mù). For those with a Metal destiny, the grave is in Chǒu; if they fall ill on a Yǐchǒu day, it is most inauspicious.
For those with a Wood destiny, the grave is in Wèi; if they fall ill on a Guǐwèi day, it is most inauspicious.
For those whose destiny is Water, the tomb is in the position of Chen; falling ill on a Ren-Chen day brings great misfortune.
For those whose destiny is Fire, the tomb is in the position of Xu; falling ill on a Jia-Xu day brings great misfortune.
For those whose destiny is Earth, the tomb is in the position of Chen; falling ill on a Bing-Chen day brings great misfortune.
The profound mechanism of this Dharma pervades heaven and earth: For the "Great Month," count from top to bottom;

for the "Small Month," count from bottom to top. First inquire about the number of months since the illness began, and one will immediately know whether the patient's condition is auspicious or ominous. This wondrous secret method of calculation is understood by no one.
In the primordial state, a hair’s breadth determines life and death; from the first day of the month, one must deliberate with meticulous care.
When the horse stands upright, human life faces disaster that can be remedied; when the horse falls, it is gathered back into the realm of darkness.
If the horse leans, there is misfortune, yet it may still be treated; if the official salary is secure and the destiny is heavy, one's life will not be harmed.
When both the *lù* (fortune) and *mǎ* (horse) are overturned, ghosts arrive at the door; when the *lù* is slanted, there is calamity—consult a physician.
When the *míng* (destiny) is upright, [the years] five, nine, two, six, and ten [are auspicious].

The four characters Zi, Wu, Mao, and You are high; Born with intelligence, he displays heroic prowess.
He has many brothers, yet they are difficult to rely upon; His parents are no longer together.
In the beginning, middle, and end, there is no companion; At this very time, he is solitary and must carry his burden alone.
Wealth is heavy, emolument honorable, and the person noble and distinguished; Wings reach the Milky Way, blessings flow like a great river.
The four characters *yin*, *shen*, *si*, and *hai* are strong; Born intelligent and wise, one draws near to literature.
At times there are three or four brothers; In the beginning and at the end, they also form pairs.
Parents have no punishment and rely heavily on their children; they enjoy honor, wealth, and nobility while seated in the high hall.
If one’s parents are both fully present, the late years will be prosperous and greatly auspicious.
The four characters *Chen*, *Xu*, *Chou*, and *Wei* constitute the "Orphan" (Gu) trigram; these afflict the parents above and distance one from their six kin.
Though there be brothers, they are difficult to rely upon; the ancestral home is constantly occupied by others.
At the beginning of one's life, one manages the estate of a deceased father; at the end of one's time, one is deprived of a mother in the realm of the dead.
One’s livelihood is found in public service; sons become monks or Daoists, and daughters become nuns.
寅 (Yin), 巳 (Si), 申 (Shen), and 亥 (Hai) are on the left;
丑 (Chou), 辰 (Chen), 未 (Wei), and 戌 (Xu) are on the right;
子 (Zi), 午 (Wu), 卯 (Mao), and 酉 (You) are the cardinal directions.
